passage: The email arrived at 4:12 p.m. while Nilesh was on a crowded Borivali local: 'After careful consideration, we have decided to move forward with other candidates.' He read it four times between stations. It had been his third round at the logistics firm, and he had already pictured the ID card. By the time he got home he had decided he simply wasn't good enough for any company. His cousin Rehana, who had been through two dozen rejections before her own job, sat with him on the building steps. 'Reply once. Ask politely what you could improve. Then pick one thing and fix it.' That night Nilesh sent a two-line email asking for feedback. The HR contact replied the next day: his case-study answer had lacked numbers. He wrote 'practise case studies with data' on a sticky note and applied to two more firms that week.

qa.q: At what time did the email arrive?
qa.a: The email arrived at 4:12 p.m.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling by the time he got home?
qa.a: Nilesh felt crushed and ashamed, convinced he wasn't good enough for any company.

qa.q: What small steps did Nilesh take after the rejection?
qa.a: He asked once for feedback, wrote down the one fix about case studies with data, and applied to two more firms.

qa.q: How does Rehana see Nilesh's rejection?
qa.a: Having faced two dozen rejections herself, Rehana sees it as one decision to learn from, not a verdict on Nilesh.

grounding: Shows a polite rejection mail that feels personal, and the wise steps of asking once for feedback, noting one fix and applying again.

passage:
'You've been replaying that interview for nine days, Damini.'
'Because I keep hearing myself say "I'm a perfectionist" like a fool.'
'Did they say that's why?'
'They didn't say anything. Just "we are moving ahead with other candidates." Very polite. Very final.'
'So you've decided it's you.'
'Who else would it be?'
'Maybe they had one seat and forty people.'
'I'm not applying anywhere else this month. I can't go through it again.'
'Okay. Deal: you write one email asking them for feedback. Just one. Then tomorrow you look at the three openings on the placement board.'
'And if they don't reply?'
'Then you've lost two minutes. And you still look at the openings.'
Damini groaned into the pillow. Then she pulled out her laptop. 'Help me word it so I don't sound desperate.'
'Pass it here,' Pooja said.

qa.q: How many days had Damini been replaying the interview?
qa.a: Damini had been replaying it for nine days.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling about the rejection?
qa.a: Damini felt embarrassed and discouraged, blaming the 'perfectionist' answer and dreading another interview.

qa.q: Why was Pooja's deal a wise one?
qa.a: One feedback email and a look at three openings stops the endless replaying and gets Damini moving again.

qa.q: How does Pooja see Damini's replaying?
qa.a: Pooja sees Damini deciding it was all Damini's fault without evidence, when many people may have applied for one seat.

grounding: Shows a rejection being replayed for days, and a friend steering toward one request for feedback and new applications.

passage: In Wardha, the only coaching centre for job exams had a noticeboard, and Alka had stopped reading it. Three weeks ago Karthik, a recruiter for a private insurance office in the district town, had called: 'You are almost selected. Just wait for the formal letter.' She had told her mother, turned down tuition work for the summer and stopped filling other forms. Then nothing. Two weeks of nothing. She went from checking her phone every hour to snapping at her little brother for borrowing it. Her old tuition teacher, Joshi-sir, heard it all at the bus stand. 'Don't stop your life for one maybe. Send two polite follow-ups, a week apart. Meanwhile fill those two forms on the board.' That evening Alka sent the first message to Karthik and filled one form at the cyber café. The second she would finish tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Karthik say when he called?
qa.a: Karthik said, 'You are almost selected. Just wait for the formal letter.'

qa.q: What was Alka feeling after two weeks of nothing?
qa.a: Alka felt confused and angry, her hope turning into irritation that she took out on her little brother.

qa.q: Why is Joshi-sir's advice wise?
qa.a: Two polite follow-ups a week apart, while filling other forms, keeps one uncertain offer from holding her whole life still.

qa.q: How might Karthik see the 'almost selected' call?
qa.a: Karthik may have said it casually or before a final decision, not realising Alka would turn down work and stop applying because of it.

grounding: Shows the hope-then-silence of an 'almost selected' promise, and the advice to keep other applications alive and follow up politely twice.

passage: Bilal, the recruiter from a design agency in Hanoi, had shaken Tuan's hand after the final round and said, 'You're almost there, we just need sign-off.' That was five weeks ago. Tuan had declined a second interview at a smaller studio because it felt like cheating on the first. He hadn't renewed his room lease properly, thinking he might move closer to the agency. He had sent one polite email in week two and heard nothing. By week five he was angry at himself as much as at Bilal. His flatmate Linh asked, 'What happens if they never call?' Tuan didn't have an answer. That night he sent a second, final follow-up, short and friendly, and then wrote to the smaller studio: 'If the role is still open, I'd love to talk.' They replied by morning. He renewed the lease for another six months.

qa.q: How many weeks ago was the final round?
qa.a: The final round was five weeks ago.

qa.q: What was Tuan feeling by week five?
qa.a: Tuan felt angry and confused, at Bilal and at himself for putting life on hold.

qa.q: What would you advise someone in Tuan's position once the first follow-up goes unanswered?
qa.a: Send one more short, polite follow-up and keep other options open, as Tuan finally did with the smaller studio.

qa.q: What does Linh's question suggest Linh sees?
qa.a: Linh sees that Tuan has frozen life around one uncertain offer and gently points to it.

grounding: Shows a candidate who froze his plans after being told he was almost selected, then followed up a final time and revived other options.

passage: Zeenat's bus from Aligarh broke down on the highway, and she reached the Noida office with eleven minutes to spare, sweat on her collar and hands like ice. In the waiting area she could hear the panel laughing behind a glass door. What if they saw she was not as good as her CV? She pressed her palms together and did the slow count her friend Irfan had taught her in exam week: in for four, out for six. Then she ran through her three stories: the college fest budget, the survey project, the time she untangled the library's printer queue. Inside, the second question was about a software tool she had never used. The urge to bluff rose. 'I haven't used it,' she said. 'But I learned our survey software in a weekend from the manual and videos. I'd do the same here.' One panellist nodded and wrote something down.

qa.q: How early did Zeenat reach the Noida office?
qa.a: Zeenat reached with eleven minutes to spare.

qa.q: What was Zeenat afraid of in the waiting area?
qa.a: Zeenat was afraid the panel would see she was not as good as her CV.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Admitting she hadn't used the tool and explaining how she would learn it, because a bluff would have collapsed on the next question.

qa.q: How might the panel see Zeenat's honest answer?
qa.a: The panel may see someone honest about gaps who knows how to learn, which is why one panellist nodded and made a note.

grounding: Shows interview fear under time pressure, met with breathing, prepared real stories and an honest 'I haven't used it, but here is how I would learn'.

passage: The night before her campus interview in Bhubaneswar, Sarika lay awake with cold feet under the blanket, sure the panel would see through her. Her hostel mate Gargi sat up. 'Tell me three things you've actually done.' Sarika listed them: the flood-relief drive she ran, the Odia-English tutoring, the internship report her manager had praised. 'Those are your answers. And if you don't know something, don't pretend.' In the interview the next morning, Sarika bluffed on the first tough question, about interest rate trends, and the follow-up left her stammering. Her face went hot. Then she remembered Gargi. 'I'm sorry, I actually don't know the recent figures. I'd check the central bank's latest report before any client meeting.' The panellist's expression softened. On the next question she told the flood-relief story, and her voice steadied.

qa.q: Where was Sarika's campus interview?
qa.a: Sarika's campus interview was in Bhubaneswar.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling after the follow-up question left her stammering?
qa.a: Sarika felt embarrassed and exposed, her face going hot.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Bluffing on interest rate trends collapsed on the follow-up; admitting she didn't know and saying how she would check it fixed it.

qa.q: How does Gargi see Sarika's fear the night before?
qa.a: Gargi sees that Sarika has real achievements and helps turn them into answers instead of letting the fear run the night.

grounding: Shows fear of being exposed before a panel, a bluff that collapses, and recovery through honesty and real stories.

passage: The message came on the group chat while Tuan was queueing for noodles near the Sydney campus: Camila had got the graduate role at the engineering firm they had both interviewed for. Tuan typed 'congrats!!' and felt two things at once: real warmth, because Camila had helped him through second-year maths, and a sour twist in his stomach. On the walk home he caught himself thinking, 'That firm's culture is terrible anyway.' He stopped at a bench and said it out loud, quietly: 'I'm jealous.' Oddly, it helped. That evening he called Camila instead of just texting. 'I'm really happy for you. And a bit jealous, honestly.' She laughed. 'I'd be too.' 'How did you prepare for the technical round?' She talked for twenty minutes. He took notes on the back of an envelope.

qa.q: Where was Tuan when the message came?
qa.a: Tuan was queueing for noodles near the Sydney campus.

qa.q: What two feelings did Tuan have on hearing Camila's news?
qa.a: Tuan felt real warmth for Camila and a sour twist of envy at the same time.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Admitting the envy, congratulating honestly and asking how Camila prepared, because it turned envy into learning instead of sneering.

qa.q: How does Camila take Tuan's honest admission?
qa.a: Camila takes it lightly and kindly, laughing that she would feel the same, then shares twenty minutes of tips.

grounding: Shows warmth and envy together when a friend gets the offer, and the wise path of admitting it, congratulating and asking how she prepared.

passage: The placement cell at the Indore college pinned the results at noon. Pranav's name was under the bank that had rejected Sunaina in the final round. Around her, classmates slapped his back. Sunaina smiled and felt something sour rise. In the corridor she heard herself tell a friend, 'That bank has terrible hours, he'll quit in six months,' and a small, mean part of her hoped he would. Back in the empty seminar room she sat with it. Pranav had shared his notes with her all year. The sour feeling wasn't about him; it was about her own no. She wrote in her notebook: 'I'm envious. That's allowed. Being unkind isn't.' At the canteen she found Pranav. 'Congratulations, really. You earned it. Can you tell me what they asked in the last round?' He looked relieved, and pulled up a chair.

qa.q: When did the placement cell pin the results?
qa.a: The placement cell pinned the results at noon.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling when she saw Pranav's name?
qa.a: Sunaina felt envious and sour, even hoping for a moment that he would quit.

qa.q: What did Sunaina do that turned the envy around?
qa.a: She named it privately in her notebook, congratulated Pranav honestly, and asked what the last round covered.

qa.q: Why might Pranav look relieved when Sunaina congratulates him?
qa.a: Pranav may have worried the result would hurt their friendship, since she had been rejected by the same bank.

grounding: Shows the sour twist of envy when a batchmate gets the offer, a moment of sneering, and then private honesty and a sincere congratulation.

passage:
Sharmila: GD round tomorrow. 8 people, 1 topic, 15 min. I plan to talk the most 💪
Nikita: talk the most or say the best thing?
Sharmila: same thing. if I don't grab the floor someone else will
Nikita: our placement senior said panels mark people who interrupt as poor team players
Sharmila: ugh. so I just sit quietly?
Nikita: no. make 2-3 clear points. and when someone says something good, build on it and say their name
Sharmila: that feels like helping the competition
Nikita: it shows you can work with people. that's literally what they're hiring for
(next evening)
Sharmila: ok update. I didn't interrupt once
Sharmila: a boy made a smart point about rural internet and I said 'building on Faisal's point' and the moderator looked up and smiled 🙂
Nikita: and??
Sharmila: shortlisted for the interview!!

qa.q: How many people were in the GD?
qa.a: There were 8 people in the GD.

qa.q: What does 'if I don't grab the floor someone else will' suggest Sharmila was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests Sharmila felt anxious and competitive, seeing the others as obstacles.

qa.q: Why did Nikita's advice work?
qa.a: Making a few clear points and building on others' ideas by name showed the panel someone who can work with others.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Faisal to hear 'building on Faisal's point'?
qa.a: Faisal would likely feel respected and included rather than shouted down, which makes the discussion better for everyone.

grounding: A chat shows a candidate who sees GD rivals as obstacles learning to make clear points and credit others instead of talking over them.

passage: The group discussion for the cooperative bank trainee posts was held in a stuffy upstairs hall in Pala, a small town in Kottayam district. Thomas had decided on the bus: be loud, be first, be remembered. When Anjali began explaining how the self-help groups in her village ran their meetings, he cut in over her: 'That's just one example, the real issue is...' A panel member tapped a pen. Thomas saw it, and saw Anjali's face close. For a few minutes he kept talking, faster, but the room had gone cold. Then he stopped. 'Sorry. Anjali, finish your point about the self-help groups, it was strong.' She did, and it was. He added two facts from his project on crop loans, and a quieter boy by the window got a turn too. Afterwards, on the stairs, Anjali said, 'Thanks for handing it back.' Thomas said, 'I shouldn't have taken it.'

qa.q: Where was the group discussion held?
qa.a: It was held in a stuffy upstairs hall in Pala.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when the panel member tapped a pen?
qa.a: Thomas felt uneasy and under pressure, talking faster as he sensed the room turning cold.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Talking over Anjali went wrong; apologising, handing the floor back and crediting her point fixed it.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt when Thomas cut in?
qa.a: Anjali likely felt dismissed and shut out, as her face closed, and later appreciated him handing it back.

grounding: Shows a candidate treating a group discussion as a fight to be heard, noticing the cost, and switching to crediting others.

passage: Every evening in their small flat in Taichung, Jin's mother asked the same question over the rice: 'Any news?' Tonight, when he shook his head, she sighed. 'Mrs. Chen's son Xin started at the electronics company last month. Already a badge, already a desk.' Jin felt his face heat. He wanted to slam his bowl down, or go silent for three days like last time. Instead he looked at her hands, the way she kept turning her chopsticks. She was worried, not cruel. 'Ma, I know you're scared I'll fall behind. Here's what I'm doing.' He took out his phone and showed her his list: two interviews next week, the online certificate finishing on the 20th, a follow-up with the shipping firm on Friday. 'Give me until the end of next month. If nothing works, we'll talk again.' His mother read the list twice, then put more fish on his plate.

qa.q: When does Jin's online certificate finish?
qa.a: Jin's online certificate finishes on the 20th.

qa.q: What was Jin feeling when his mother mentioned Xin?
qa.a: Jin felt small and angry, his face heating, tempted to slam his bowl or go silent.

qa.q: What made Jin's response wise?
qa.a: He saw the worry under the comparison, shared a clear plan with dates, and asked for time until the end of next month.

qa.q: What does putting more fish on Jin's plate suggest about his mother?
qa.a: It suggests she feels reassured by the plan and is showing care without words.

grounding: Shows a parent comparing a job-seeking son with the neighbour's son, and Jin hearing the worry underneath and sharing a dated plan.

passage: On visiting day at the engineering hostel in Roorkee, Wasim's father sat stiffly on a plastic chair and unwrapped the tiffin Ammi had sent. 'Jatin from next door got placed at the cement company,' he said. 'His father distributed sweets in the whole lane.' Wasim stared at the floor. Two rejections this month, and now this, in the visiting room with other families listening. Last semester he had shouted, and they hadn't spoken for a week. He breathed out. 'Abbu, you're worried I'll be left behind. I'm worried too.' His father looked up. Wasim opened his notebook: three companies coming on the 12th, 18th and 25th; mock interviews with the placement cell every Tuesday; a backup plan for the master's entrance in February. 'Be patient with me till March.' His father closed the tiffin slowly. 'March,' he said, and pushed the kebabs toward his son.

qa.q: On which dates are the three companies coming?
qa.a: The companies are coming on the 12th, 18th and 25th.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling as he stared at the floor?
qa.a: Wasim felt small and hurt, embarrassed with other families listening after two rejections that month.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than last semester's shouting, and why?
qa.a: Naming his father's worry and showing a dated plan, because it answered the fear under the comparison.

qa.q: How might Wasim's father see the moment when Wasim names the worry?
qa.a: Wasim's father may feel understood and less anxious, which is why he agrees to March and pushes the kebabs toward his son.

grounding: Shows a father comparing Wasim with the neighbour's placed son, and Wasim answering the worry with a dated plan instead of shouting.

passage: Hostel warden's log, Tuesday night. Around 9, I saw Omkar, final-year commerce, sitting on the back steps near the water cooler, still in his interview shirt. Earlier he had told the desk he'd heard back from the audit firm; from his face, it was a no. Payal from the girls' block came and sat one step below him. She didn't give a speech. She passed him a packet of peanuts and stayed. At one point he said, 'You don't have to sit here, I'm fine,' and she said, 'I know. I'm sitting anyway.' After about twenty minutes his shoulders came down. I heard him laugh once. Before curfew he said he would email the firm for feedback in the morning. I checked in with him on my round at 10:30; he said he was going to sleep. I'll look in on him at breakfast tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Payal pass to Omkar?
qa.a: Payal passed him a packet of peanuts.

qa.q: What might Omkar have been feeling when he said 'You don't have to sit here, I'm fine'?
qa.a: Omkar likely felt hurt and embarrassed, perhaps unworthy of comfort, and tried to wave it away.

qa.q: What small next step did Omkar choose after being comforted?
qa.a: Omkar decided to email the firm for feedback in the morning.

qa.q: How does Payal seem to see Omkar's rejection?
qa.a: Payal sees that Omkar needs company more than advice, so she simply stays without trying to fix it.

grounding: A warden's log shows a friend sitting quietly with Omkar after a rejection, and Omkar accepting the comfort and taking one small next step.

passage: Wednesday. Diary, it's Shankar. The newspaper firm said no this morning. I'd been so sure. I wanted to hide in my room all day. Siddharth came over at lunch with two cutting chais and didn't ask a single question. He just sat on my floor and read a comic while I stared at the ceiling. Once I started saying, 'You should go, I'm bad company, I don't deserve you wasting your afternoon,' and he said, 'Drink your chai,' and kept reading. Somewhere in the second hour I started talking. About the interview, about Appa's face when I told him. Siddharth only nodded. By four I could breathe properly again. When he left, I did one small thing: I opened the list of openings and saved one, the magazine internship. Just saved it. Tomorrow I'll write the cover letter.

qa.q: What did Siddharth bring at lunch?
qa.a: Siddharth brought two cutting chais.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling when saying 'I don't deserve you wasting your afternoon'?
qa.a: Shankar felt low and undeserving of kindness after the rejection, wanting to push the comfort away.

qa.q: What small next step did Shankar take after the afternoon?
qa.a: Shankar saved the magazine internship opening and planned to write the cover letter tomorrow.

qa.q: How does Siddharth seem to see Shankar's rejection?
qa.a: Siddharth sees that Shankar needs company, not questions or fixes, so he just stays and lets Shankar talk when ready.

grounding: A diary shows a friend sitting through a rejection without rushing to fix it, Shankar nearly refusing the comfort, then accepting it and taking one step.

passage:
'Pranav-bhaiya, got a minute?'
'Kishore! How did the interview go?'
'That's why I'm here. First, thank you. Properly. That mock interview on Saturday was brutal.'
'Too brutal?'
'No. When you said my answers sounded like I'd memorised a website, I wanted to disappear.'
'Sorry about that.'
'Don't be. I went home and rewrote all of them with my own examples. The canteen inventory thing, the robotics club budget. And today when they asked about teamwork, I told the robotics story.'
'And?'
'They asked me three follow-ups on it. They were actually interested.'
'That's great, man.'
'Second round is Friday. Can I tell you how it goes?'
'You'd better. Most people take the mock and I never hear from them again.'
Kishore grinned, a bit red in the face. 'Not me, bhaiya.'

qa.q: When is Kishore's second round?
qa.a: The second round is Friday.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when Pranav said the answers sounded memorised?
qa.a: Kishore felt embarrassed and hurt, wanting to disappear, though Kishore is now grateful for it.

qa.q: What made Kishore's thank-you meaningful?
qa.a: Kishore applied the feedback by rewriting answers with real examples, came back to report, and promised to share how Friday goes.

qa.q: How does Pranav see Kishore coming back?
qa.a: Pranav is pleased and a little surprised, since most people take the mock and never report back.

grounding: Shows gratitude to a senior whose honest mock-interview feedback stung, expressed by thanking him, using the feedback and reporting back.

passage: I'm Himani, and I still go a bit red remembering Ojas's feedback. He was two years senior, already working at a consulting firm, and he gave up his Sunday to do a mock interview with me over a video call. At the end he said, very kindly, 'You speak fast when you're nervous, and you never actually answered why you want this job.' I said thank you, closed the laptop and cried a little. For a week I didn't reply to his follow-up message, because I was embarrassed. Then I realised that vanishing after someone gives you their Sunday is rude. So I wrote to him: what I'd changed, that I'd practised slowing down with a timer, and that my real answer to 'why this job' was my father's small printing shop. I got the offer in March. Ojas was the second person I called.

qa.q: What did Ojas give up to do the mock interview?
qa.a: Ojas gave up his Sunday.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling in the week after the mock interview?
qa.a: Himani felt embarrassed and a little hurt, which is why the follow-up message went unanswered for a week.

qa.q: What did Himani do right in the end?
qa.a: Himani wrote to thank Ojas, explained what had changed, like practising slowing down with a timer, and later called with the news.

qa.q: How might Ojas have felt getting Himani's message after a week of silence?
qa.a: Ojas was likely glad and reassured that the feedback helped and that his Sunday had been worth it.

grounding: A first-person account of thankful embarrassment after a senior's honest mock interview, and choosing to report back rather than vanish.

passage:
Day 1: After the fourth rejection, Avni sat in the college library in Nagpur and listed the reasons: 'Quotas. Connections. They only want convent-school English.' Her classmate Akash, turned down by two of the same firms, nodded along. It felt good to be angry together.
Day 9: Avni skipped the mock interview session. 'What's the point, the system's rigged,' she told Akash. He went anyway.
Day 20: Akash got a call-back. Over chai he said the mock panel had helped him slow down. Avni went home and wrote two lists. On one: what really is unfair, like the firm that only visited English-medium colleges. On the other: what she could change, her nervous speed, her thin project list. She kept both. The next Tuesday she went to the mock session, and joined the speaking club too, not because her accent was wrong, but to feel steadier.

qa.q: What did Avni skip on Day 9?
qa.a: Avni skipped the mock interview session.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling on Day 9 when she skipped the session?
qa.a: Avni felt bitter and defeated, sure the system was rigged and effort was pointless.

qa.q: Why were Avni's two lists a wise step?
qa.a: They let her name what is truly unfair without making it the whole story, and pick things she could control, like her speed and projects.

qa.q: How might Akash's call-back have affected Avni?
qa.a: Seeing Akash get a call-back after the mock panel showed Avni that effort still counted, which helped her move.

grounding: Shows resentment at an unfair system turning into skipped effort, then Avni separating what is unfair from what she can control.

passage: Arohi, you say the interviews are rigged. Maybe some are. Let your Sahil-chacha tell you about my own year of that. I was twenty-one, from a Hindi-medium school in Gorakhpur, and in Delhi every panel seemed to smile at my accent. Four rejections. I decided it was all the system: English, contacts, surnames. Some of that was true; one panel really did ask only about my father's job. But for a whole year I applied nowhere. I sat at the paan shop complaining with two other boys. Then my friend Ghosh, rejected as often as me, got a job at a printing press by walking in with a folder of his work. I asked him how. He said, 'The unfair part isn't mine to fix today. My folder is.' I made a folder the next week. So be angry about what's unfair, Arohi. Then make your folder.

qa.q: Where was Sahil's school?
qa.a: Sahil went to a Hindi-medium school in Gorakhpur.

qa.q: How did young Sahil feel during the year he stopped applying?
qa.a: Sahil felt bitter and resentful, blaming the whole system and giving up on effort.

qa.q: What turning point in the story got Sahil moving again?
qa.a: Seeing Ghosh get a job by walking in with a folder of work, and hearing that the folder, not the unfairness, was his to fix that day.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Ghosh to keep trying after so many rejections?
qa.a: Ghosh likely felt the same unfairness but chose to focus on what he could control, which is why he walked in with a folder.

grounding: An uncle recalls blaming the system after rejections, some of it fairly, until a friend showed him how to name the unfairness and still control what he could.

passage: Note for my own file, Thursday. Manjula, senior analyst. At this morning's team meeting, Mr. Rao held up Siddharth's report and said, 'My nephew in Class 8 could do better. I'm just being direct.' Some people laughed. Siddharth, who joined as a trainee in June, went red to the ears and stared at the table without moving. It is the third time this month I have seen Mr. Rao do this to him. After the meeting I found him at the pantry and told him plainly that this was Mr. Rao's behaviour, not a measure of his work. I suggested he write down each incident with the date and the words, and offered to go with him to HR next week as a witness. Before leaving he asked if I knew of openings in other teams or firms; I said I'd keep an ear out. I have started noting the dates myself.

qa.q: When did Siddharth join?
qa.a: Siddharth joined as a trainee in June.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling as he stared at the table?
qa.a: Siddharth felt humiliated and frozen, red to the ears after being mocked in front of the team.

qa.q: Why were Manjula's suggestions wise?
qa.a: Writing down each incident with dates, going to HR with a witness, and keeping an ear out for openings protect Siddharth and build options.

qa.q: How does Mr. Rao seem to see his own comments?
qa.a: Mr. Rao presents the mockery as just being direct, ignoring how it humiliates a new trainee.

grounding: A senior colleague's note records a boss mocking a trainee in public, and the steps of naming it as the boss's conduct, keeping dated notes, going to HR and looking for exits.

passage: Friday. Diary, Anirban here, and my face still feels hot. Today Mr. Kapoor made me read my client email aloud in the meeting and then said, 'Now say it in English,' and everyone laughed. He calls it 'toughening us up'. I just stood there. In the washroom I nearly typed my resignation on my phone. Instead I called Anjali, my college friend who's been working two years longer than me. She said three things: write down what happened today with the time and exact words; talk to Ruchika-ma'am from the other team, who everyone trusts; and meanwhile update my CV without telling anyone.
